Skydance Shares Fall 9% as Warner Bros. Films Weigh on Earnings
sum: Walt Disney shares fell 1% in morning trading as Skydance dropped 9% despite beating quarterly earnings estimates. Skydance’s chief financial officer warned that underperforming Warner Bros. films would weigh on fourth-quarter adjusted earnings, while Disney’s decline was smaller than the newly merged company’s.

Walt Disney shares fell 1% in morning trading as Skydance stock dropped 9% after its chief financial officer warned that underperforming Warner Bros. films would drag fourth-quarter adjusted earnings by $200 million. Disney stock was trading at $117.64, while Skydance shares stood at $7.92.

Skydance’s decline came despite the company beating analysts’ estimates for its first quarterly results since completing its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The contrasting share moves pointed to concerns focused on Skydance’s film slate and balance sheet rather than a broad selloff across media stocks.
Skydance reported adjusted earnings per share of $0.45, above the $0.20 consensus estimate. Revenue reached $7.03 billion, compared with a $7.02 billion estimate, and rose 4.8% year over year.

On a GAAP basis, Skydance earned $0.06 per share. Its results included $89 million in restructuring costs, $98 million in transaction-related costs and a $275 million discrete tax reserve, partly offset by a $514 million net derivative gain.

Chief Financial Officer Dennis Cinelli said the Warner Bros. film slate would create a $200 million drag on adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization in the fourth quarter. The impact covers films already released and those still due before the quarter ends.

Skydance’s streaming and studio businesses grew, with Paramount+ revenue up 21% and Studios revenue up 23% on secondary licensing. Television revenue fell 7%, however, while advertising declined 8% and affiliate revenue dropped 5% amid pay-TV subscriber erosion.

sum: This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

A clean earnings beat is taking a back seat to a weaker studio outlook at the newly combined home of Warner Bros. and Paramount. Skydance (NYSE:SKYD) stock is at $7.92 in morning trading, down 9%. The company, formerly Paramount Skydance, completed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery on October 6, so Warner Bros. Discovery shares no longer trade separately.
Skydance stock is also down 40% year to date (YTD). Results for Q3 2026, released after the close on November 9, were the first for the merged company.

Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) at Skydance came in at $0.45, beating the $0.20 consensus estimate. Quarterly revenue at Skydance reached $7.03 billion, exceeding the $7.02 billion consensus and growing 4.8% year over year. On a GAAP basis, the company earned $0.06 per share after $89 million in restructuring costs, $98 million in transaction-related costs and a $275 million discrete tax reserve, partly offset by a $514 million net derivative gain.

Growth at Paramount+ was strong, with revenue up 21%, while Studios revenue rose 23% on secondary licensing. Skydance’s Warner Bros. film slate keeps underperforming. CFO Dennis Cinelli said that will create a $200 million drag to Q4 2026 adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, covering films already released and those still due before the quarter ends.

Skydance Chairman and CEO David Ellison repeated a target of at least $6 billion in run-rate synergies within three years and more than $10 billion in free cash flow by 2030. “Growing our business and paying down debt are our top priorities, and we strongly believe we can achieve both simultaneously,” Ellison said. A Paramount+ and HBO Max bundle is planned for early 2027, and Ellison named Jeremy Latcham, whom he called “one of the founding team members of Marvel Studios,” to the DC studio operation.

Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX | NFLX Price Prediction) stock is at $62.90, down 2%. Meanwhile, Walt Disney (NYSE:DIS) stock is trading at $117.64, down 1%. Both moves are modest next to Skydance’s decline, which points to company-specific worries about its Warner Bros. film slate and balance sheet.

items.t: Dancing With the Stars ’ Adele Zaikman Shares Why She's Missing Disney Night
sum: Even a wish upon a star won’t get Adele Zaikman into the ballroom.

While the Dancing With the Stars pro, who was partnered with Connor Leavitt before their week one exit, has been a key member of the eliminated cohort that performs during show breaks, she's recently been sidelined by an illness.

“I’m sadly feeling unwell and won’t be performing in the opening number on Dancing With the Stars tomorrow,” the 25-year-old wrote in a since-expired Instagram Story Nov. 1. “I’m so sad to miss a show day, but I’ll be taking this time to take care of myself. Sending so much love to everyone on that ballroom floor. I’ll be cheering you on from home.”
Because she’s under the weather, Zaikman—who earned a season 35 spot by placing first on Dancing With the Stars: The Next Pro—will miss the Nov. 2's Disney-themed night.
And even though the road is looking rough ahead, Zaikman’s got many friends willing to stick together and help her see it through.

“I think that I'm the luckiest human on earth,” she said in a video shared to her Story later that day, adding that her friend Brenda “just stopped by just to give me this superfood honey and things that help me with my cough and some special teas.”
Not only that, but the good friend also dropped off some blueberry muffins. “How good do they look?” Zaikman stressed. “I mean, I am so lucky that I have people like that in my life.”

Unpacking Q2 Earnings: Disney (NYSE:DIS) In The Context Of Other Consumer Discretionary - Media Stocks
sum: As the Q2 earnings season comes to a close, it's time to take stock of this quarter's best and worst performers in the consumer discretionary - media industry, including Disney (NYSE:DIS) and its peers.

The Consumer Discretionary sector, by definition, is made up of companies selling non-essential goods and services. When economic conditions deteriorate or tastes shift, consumers can easily cut back or eliminate these purchases. For long-term investors with five-year holding periods, this creates a structural challenge: the sector is inherently hit-driven, with low switching costs and fickle customers. As a result, only a handful of companies can reliably grow demand and compound earnings over long periods, which is why our bar is high and High Quality ratings are rare.Media companies create, aggregate, and distribute content—including news, entertainment, and advertising—across television, print, digital, and out-of-home channels. Tailwinds include growing digital advertising budgets, content licensing opportunities, and global audience expansion through streaming and social platforms. Headwinds are substantial: traditional advertising revenue from print and linear TV continues its structural decline as audiences migrate to digital alternatives. Content creation costs are escalating amid intense competition for talent and intellectual property. Media fragmentation makes it difficult to build sustainable audience scale, while AI-generated content threatens to commoditize production and disrupt established business models.
The 7 consumer discretionary - media stocks we track reported a satisfactory Q2. As a group, revenues missed analysts' consensus estimates by 0.8%.
In light of this news, share prices of the companies have held steady. On average, they are relatively unchanged since the latest earnings results.

Why Is Walt Disney Stock So Much Cheaper Than Netflix? This Is the Only Answer I Can Think Of.
sum: Walt Disney (DIS -0.40%) shares have tumbled. They now trade 52% below their record from March 2021 as of July 20, at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 15.4. But the business is performing well from a fundamental perspective.
Netflix (NFLX -3.28%) has also faltered. Its shares are 50% off their peak from June 2025. However, they trade at a P/E ratio of 21.3, 38% more expensive than Disney.

Investors who have followed Disney for a while know that the stock can never sustainably command a high valuation multiple from the investment community. That's particularly true right now. I believe there are two headwinds that pressure the stock.

The market probably continues to punish the stock because Disney's cable networks, a dying offering, are still a material part of the overall business. During fiscal 2025 (ended Sept. 27, 2025), this segment generated 10% of the company's total revenue and 17% of its operating income.

To be clear, these figures have continued to come down, but they highlight an anchor that prevents Disney from truly letting go of its past. This situation creates a financial impediment, as gains in other segments have to work harder to offset the secular decline of cable TV.
Another headwind relates to the nature of this company. Disney has always been a capital-intensive business. Creating and acquiring content is particularly expensive.

In the physical world, the theme parks and cruise ships require significant capital to maintain and grow. This reality isn't changing, and it sucks up capital that could be returned to shareholders in the form of higher dividends and stock buybacks.
